newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto Stock Exchange closing trading floor.
newsitem.headline: Toronto Stock Exchange closing trading floor.

text.p: After years of delays, the Toronto Stock Exchange will shut its trading floor for good this week -- a much-touted step that has not met with universal delight from traders.

Jettisoning the 30,000-square-foot floor on Wednesday will save the TSE about C$4 million ($2.9 million) a year in real estate costs, and result in priceless efficiency gains, Chief Executive Rowland Fleming said on Monday.

"We have advanced from chalkboards through to the floorless trading environment. The capacity of that floorless trading system is in theory infinite compared to the capacity of a floored trading environment," Fleming said in an interview.

The TSE, founded in 1861, is the world's seventh largest equities exchange, and the biggest in North America to relinquish its floor. It is a road the much larger New York Stock Exchange has no plans to travel because it swears by the face-to-face method of trade.

"The system is already highly automated in the delivery of orders and the processing of orders, but it does provide for human interaction at the point of sale, which enables people to bring their judgment and risk-taking to the process," NYSE spokesman Ray Pellecchia said.

Toronto's long-awaited move to floorless trading has invoked nostalgia among traders. It has also prompted fears that market volatility could increase, while leaving some veteran floor traders feeling saddened and displaced.

Jimmy Taugher, 66, a professional bank stock trader, eyes his computer screen dubiously and scratches numbers on a white pad. But in Taugher's 44-year working life, he has logged just two weeks in an office.

"I miss the noise. I liked the excitement, the way things happened...the floor was fun. And it makes a big difference if you can have fun when you work," Taugher of the Independent Trading Group, said in an interview.

Some dealers have settled in more readily. The migration of stocks to the TSE CATS computer system from the floor system has been ongoing since the start of 1997 and traders have left the floor for their brokerages when the stocks they monitored left their trading floor "posts".
Only one TSE trading post remains, so most floor traders already work from their brokerage desks.
"At first, I think that people were upset about having our way of life changed," said Joe Hannan, 55, a floor trader at W.D. Latimer Co. who moved to a desk more than a month ago.
"But everybody's accepted that this is the way it is. It's the 90s. Everything's computerized," he added.
By the end of 1997, trading will all be on a system purchased from the Paris Bourse. Now it is split between the new system, called Torex, and the older CATS system.
The gaudy identifying jackets and the "open outcry" shouts faded into memory years ago, but the floor retained a camaraderie and what some consider a healthy haggling process.

The loss of face-to-face contact as traders move to a pure computer-based system may boost volatility, traders believe. They said that buying and selling will be executed in a vacuum, with traders unable to cushion big price swings in thinly traded stocks.
But Fleming dismissed this argument as "specious".
"Any careful analysis of what really occurs in the New York trading environment would demonstrate that the amount of human intervention is actually quite minimal," he said.
"If you look at the list of large exchanges in the world, the majority of them are floorless," he added, citing as examples floorless markets in London, Sydney, Paris and Hong Kong.
Many believe the floor closing may also hurt the visibility of the Toronto exchange. But the TSE has a solution for that.
Fleming said the exchange planned to set up an 8,000- square-foot visitor center with high-technology exhibits focused on investor education.
